cls: Herbal medicinal product - standardised Ginkgo biloba leaf extract
pharm: A standardised extract of Ginkgo biloba leaves (flavone glycosides and terpene lactones) used as a herbal remedy for symptoms of mild cognitive impairment/dementia and peripheral arterial disease; not FDA-approved
quick: Standardised extract (e.g. EGb 761) 120-240 mg/day orally in 1-3 divided doses
May be taken with or without food
Avoid - safety not established and possible bleeding risk
summary: Ginkgo biloba is a standardised herbal extract of Ginkgo biloba leaves (typically standardised to about 22-27% flavone glycosides and 5-7% terpene lactones, e.g. the EGb 761 extract). It is used as a traditional/herbal medicinal product for symptoms of age-related mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia, and for symptoms of peripheral arterial occlusive disease (intermittent claudication), vertigo and tinnitus of vascular origin. A typical adult dose of standardised extract is 120-240 mg per day in one to three divided doses. It is NOT an FDA-approved drug (marketed in the US as a dietary supplement; in Europe it has herbal/EMA monograph status), so dosing follows EMA/HMPC monographs and the BNF/herbal references rather than an FDA label. Its main clinical concern is an increased bleeding tendency, especially when combined with anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents or NSAIDs; raw seeds and high doses can also lower the seizure threshold.
indications: Symptomatic relief in mild dementia / age-associated cognitive impairment (improving cognitive symptoms and quality of life)
Symptoms of peripheral arterial occlusive disease (intermittent claudication) as adjunctive therapy
Vertigo and tinnitus of presumed vascular/involutional origin (traditional use)

dosage.d: Standardised extract 120-240 mg/day orally in 1-3 divided doses
dosage.t: Oral, with or without food; effects may take several weeks
dosage.n: Use a standardised extract (e.g. EGb 761); benefit modest and debated

dosage.d: Standardised extract typically 120-240 mg/day in divided doses
dosage.n: Adjunct to exercise and risk-factor management
Traditional indication; trial for a defined period and review

admin: Use a standardised leaf extract; potency and quality of unstandardised products vary widely
Take orally, with or without food; allow several weeks of regular use before judging cognitive benefit
Do NOT consume raw or roasted ginkgo seeds/nuts - they contain ginkgotoxin and can cause seizures and poisoning
Stop at least 1-2 weeks before elective surgery because of bleeding risk
Review the need for continued use periodically
Disclose use to all prescribers, especially if on anticoagulants, antiplatelets or anticonvulsants
moa: Standardised Ginkgo biloba extract contains flavonoid glycosides (antioxidant, free-radical scavenging) and terpene lactones (ginkgolides and bilobalide). Ginkgolides antagonise platelet-activating factor, contributing to antiplatelet/rheological effects, while the flavonoids exert antioxidant activity and the extract is reported to improve microcirculation, vasoregulation and neuronal tolerance to hypoxia/ischaemia. These combined vasoactive, antioxidant and neuroprotective actions are proposed to underlie its modest symptomatic effects in cognitive and circulatory disorders, though the precise clinical mechanism remains incompletely defined.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to Ginkgo biloba preparations
relative: Concomitant anticoagulant, antiplatelet or high-dose NSAID therapy
Upcoming surgery or invasive procedures (stop beforehand)
monitor: Signs of bleeding or easy bruising

preg: Use during pregnancy should be avoided. Safety has not been established, and the antiplatelet/bleeding effect raises theoretical concerns around delivery; some constituents have uncertain reproductive safety. Recommend non-use unless a clinician judges benefit to outweigh risk.
lact: Use during breastfeeding should be avoided because of insufficient safety data on excretion into milk and effects on the infant.
renal: No established dose adjustment in renal impairment; clinical data are limited, so use with general caution.
hepatic: No established dose adjustment; rare reports of hepatic reactions to herbal products mean it should be used with caution in significant liver disease, and stopped if hepatic injury is suspected.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs) and antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel) - increased bleeding risk (additive antiplatelet/PAF-antagonist effect)
Other drugs that increase bleeding (NSAIDs, SSRIs) - additive haemorrhage risk
moderate: Anticonvulsants - ginkgotoxin (mainly in seeds/contaminated extract) may lower seizure threshold and reduce anticonvulsant efficacy
Antidiabetic agents - possible alteration of glucose control (variable reports)
CYP substrates - ginkgo may modestly affect some CYP-metabolised drugs (e.g. via CYP2C19 induction)
minor: Possible additive effects with other vasoactive herbals
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; avoid ginkgo seeds/nuts (toxic)
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; moderate intake advised
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong bleeding time; can affect coagulation tests/INR when combined with anticoagulants

serious: Bleeding events (including, rarely, intracranial or ocular haemorrhage), especially with antithrombotic drugs
Seizures (mainly from raw seeds or contaminated/high-dose products)
rare: Allergic skin reactions (the fruit pulp can cause severe contact dermatitis)

monitoring: Signs of bleeding or unusual bruising, particularly with anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Symptomatic response (cognition, claudication, tinnitus) to justify continued use
counsel: This is a herbal extract, not an FDA-approved medicine - tell every prescriber you take it
It can increase the risk of bleeding, especially with aspirin, warfarin or other blood thinners - report unusual bruising or bleeding
Stop taking it at least 1-2 weeks before any planned surgery or dental procedure
Never eat raw or roasted ginkgo seeds/nuts - they can be poisonous and cause seizures
Use a standardised product and give it several weeks before judging any benefit
pk: Symptomatic effects develop gradually over weeks of regular use
Plasma terpene lactones peak roughly 1-3 hours after an oral dose
Terpene lactone components have half-lives of about 3-10 hours
Single-dose effect a few hours; clinical benefit requires sustained daily use
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture and light, in the original container
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - marketed as a dietary supplement in the US; dosing follows EMA/HMPC herbal monographs and BNF (typical 120-240 mg/day standardised extract)
Main clinical risk is bleeding via platelet-activating-factor antagonism - caution with anticoagulants/antiplatelets and stop before surgery
Raw/roasted ginkgo seeds contain ginkgotoxin and can cause seizures and poisoning - distinct from the standardised leaf extract
Clinical evidence for cognitive/dementia benefit is modest and inconsistent
Quality and standardisation of products vary widely - prefer well-characterised extracts such as EGb 761
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume your usual schedule. Do not double up. Because benefit depends on regular use, try to take it consistently.
overdose: Excessive intake of the extract may cause gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness and an increased bleeding tendency. Ingestion of ginkgo seeds/nuts can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning with vomiting and seizures. Management is supportive: monitor for bleeding and neurological effects, control seizures with benzodiazepines, and provide general supportive care; there is no specific antidote.
